Preliminary structural survey: This initial slice-based study did not establish map flow. Its flow claims remain hypotheses. The subsequent investigation in MAPS.md and research/flow includes 3D reconstruction with patches, original AAS links, moving states, physical route checks and live-game observations.

FRAGONY / DESIGN REFERENCE / 2 NOVEMBER 2026

Learning arena map design
from Elite Force

Make movement a sequence of worthwhile decisions. Architecture, health placement, exposure and spawn rules must work together to produce those decisions.

Study of 19 supplied Holomatch source maps and two personally selected standouts, Reservoir and reverse Voyager. The custom maps receive extra weight as taste references. The supplied packages identify Reservoir as an EF2 remake by [SFI]Valix and reverse Voyager as Lady Sarah’s EF1 reverse-CTF conversion of CTF_VOY2. This collection is not a complete expansion archive.

Design lessonsOur health economyCase studiesDesign and validation21 map atlasEvidence and limits

What I will carry into the next map

  1. Design the choices before the rooms. Describe the principal fight, a recovery circuit, and a route that counters the strongest position. Then give each a recognizable spatial form. A diagram full of connected rooms is only a starting point.
  2. Different routes need different consequences. A direct crossing can save time while exposing the player; a bent edge route can break pursuit while taking longer; an upper route can give information while revealing the player to a second angle. Parallel paths with identical costs add distance without adding strategy.
  3. Verticality must change the encounter. A balcony should overlook a specific fight, be challenged from somewhere else, and have readable access and escape. A bridge over a real lower route creates a different choice from a platform beside it. Count useful interactions between heights, not the number of floors.
  4. Break views with architecture. Room offsets, thick thresholds, stairs and bends should limit what a player can see at once. Place cover after those large relationships work. Judge each high position by the information it grants and the angles or travel commitments it exposes.
  5. Separate desirable things. The 50 HP pickup, best firing position, safest recovery and most useful shortcut should not all belong to one easy circuit. Fragment routes can rival the major reward in health value; they also need exposure or travel costs.
  6. Make routes legible as spaces. Use a memorable room shape, ceiling height, large prop or silhouette at each main decision. Distinctive geometry should do most of the orientation work before color labels and floor graphics.
  7. Treat spawns as part of the layout. Cover, facing, exits and reinforcement timing change the effective map. Judge spawn safety and useful re-entry separately. Neither equal spacing nor a large spawn count guarantees either.
  8. Prove actual use. Connected navigation is necessary. Watch real movement, pursuit, healing and combat to find unused routes, monopolized platforms and repeated spawn pressure. Bot preferences can conceal good geometry or make weak geometry look busy.

The sightline and landmark principles agree with designer Josh Foreman’s PvP design account; the specific applications here are deductions from the supplied maps and Fragony’s rules.

Build circulation with exactly three pickups

Fixed user requirements: 5 HP fragments can overheal and often form lines or clusters; 25 HP pickups cannot overheal; each map has exactly one highly contested 50 HP pickup, which can overheal. No armor, ammunition, weapon or additional powerup pickups are proposed.

PickupReason to seek itSpatial jobFailure to watch for
5 HP fragmentsUseful below the overheal cap, including at full normal health.Make a route worth traversing. Lines can lead around a room edge, across an exposed balcony or through a secondary circuit.A sheltered line that respawns under a dominant platform can become the strongest sustain source.
25 HP recoveryValuable when wounded; no benefit once normal health is reached.Give an injured player a deliberate detour, a sightline break and a way back into play.Healthy opponents have no health incentive to visit. If the area has no other tactical purpose, it becomes a dead end.
One 50 HP majorA compact large heal that remains desirable above normal health.Anchor a recurring fight with multiple meaningful approaches, visible commitment to collect, and an exit to fight for.A reward protected by its own controlling perch encourages waiting rather than contesting.

Existing-code discrepancy: Test Works still defines two legacy focus-recharge pickups, assembly-focus and core-focus. They conflict with the user’s three-pickup rule and are excluded from this design model. They were recorded for a separate cleanup; this study does not alter gameplay.

Evaluate health over a route, not one pickup at a time

Ten fragments provide the same nominal 50 HP as the major. Five provide 25 HP and retain overheal value. A three-second safe fragment circuit can be stronger than an exposed 50 HP crossing; the denominator is travel time, risk and availability. Avoid a universal formula that makes every route equal: we want different situational strengths.

The current implementation caps overheal at 200 HP (or a higher normal maximum), respawns fragments and 25 HP packs after 15 seconds, and respawns the major after 30 seconds. Those are current code values, not new requirements. Thus a large fragment line can replenish twice as often as the major. Compare total obtainable health on competing circuits and how much one position can deny.

Example with a 100 HP normal maximum and 200 HP overheal cap: at 90 HP, a 25 HP pack yields only 10; a 50 HP pack yields 50; ten collected fragments yield 50. At 150 HP, the 25 HP pack yields zero, while either overheal option still yields 50. This is why the 25 HP route primarily serves recovery, while fragments also support preparation and territorial rotation.

A starting health layout for an original arena

Put the one 50 HP pickup on a contested crossing or lower pocket visible from more than one approach. Give the upper challenger access to the fight, but require it to leave its best firing position to collect. Put a fragment line on a longer peripheral rotation, with partial exposure along the collection path. Place 25 HP packs on separate broken-sightline recovery branches that return to circulation. These are blockout hypotheses to test, not fixed counts or mandatory symmetry.

What the supplied layouts teach

Reservoir — different heights can have different jobs

Measured: the main arena contains 12 deathmatch spawns, 26 small-health placements, 8 small-shield placements and 2 medium shields. Its ordinary flags are near native Z +8; the one-flag objective is at Z −832. Small-health placements all sit at Z −167. Weapon entities range from Z −797 to +19. Nine ladder entities are present; this does not mean nine independent shafts. Eighteen additional deathmatch starts are in disconnected specialty rooms far below the arena.

Read from the sections: the low reservoir footprint, divided middle geometry and upper objective zone create distinct spatial layers rather than one floor repeated at different heights. The lower route creates a substantial commitment. The higher slice exposes lateral spaces that are absent in the low slice.

Application: preserve the contrast between a visible contest, a lateral rotation and a lower escape or recovery route. Our lift replacements change the time and vulnerability of source ladder travel, so geometry fidelity alone cannot preserve the original balance. The current port converts the 26 small-health and 8 small-shield positions into 34 fragments, the 2 medium shields into 25 HP packs, then adds six 25 HP packs and one central 50 HP major. That conversion needs a health-circuit audit, not an assumption that original placement automatically balances FFA.

Project evidence: prior local flow checks recorded base-heavy activity and no gallery visits before spawn and AI changes. The later three-match regression recorded combat in all six named regions, but gallery shot totals remained much smaller than base and center totals. That proves an improvement in use; it does not prove equal tactical value or human enjoyment.

Reverse Voyager — starts can rewrite the game

Measured: the BSP contains 24 deathmatch starts, all at native Z 88; both flags are at Z 200. The 14 red initial team starts are 829–1057 units in straight-line distance from the blue flag but 2785–3014 from the red flag; blue starts show the corresponding reversal. These are geometric distances, not route times. There are eight target_teleporter entities, connected by named targets to six target_position destinations.

Interpretation: the package’s reverse-CTF description is corroborated by the start/flag arrangement. Spawn identity changes who is near which objective, while teleport relationships supplement ordinary spatial distance. The sections show an elongated repeated end-to-end structure with pickups distributed along its length.

Application: borrow the layered approaches and recognizable ends; evaluate FFA spawns independently. A deathmatch start on the lower plane is not automatically a safe or useful arrival point. Teleport and other non-walking links must be explicit, directed edges when comparing arrival times. This is CTF_VOY2’s conversion; it is not the stock HM_VOY2 map.

Borg 1 — compact does not have to mean flat

Measured: eight deathmatch starts occupy four distinct origin heights from −232 to +32. Two combat-armor placements sit at heights +16 and −112. The horizontal sections change from a compact, divided lower space to smaller upper footprints around the same bounds.

Application: prototype a small multi-height combat volume with route alternatives before increasing the footprint. Split recovery and vantage incentives between levels, and provide counterplay against the upper approach. The presence of teleport entities means a walking-only sketch would miss part of the connection structure.

Raven — height is one tool, not a requirement

Measured: all eleven deathmatch starts are at Z 24; all spawn, weapon, health and armor origins lie within a 48-unit vertical band. The lower slice shows several partitioned volumes along an extended spine. The two body armors are at (−432, −1016, 16) and (1208, −1088, 16), separated by about 1642 units horizontally.

Application: room subdivision, branching, thresholds and separated incentives can create decisions even with little vertical spread. Do not add another floor unless it improves combat. The 48-unit band describes these entity origins, not the full height of every walkable surface.

Temple and Voyager 2 — study the stacked reward structure

Measured: Temple’s nine starts span seven distinct heights; body armors are at Z −180 and +240. Its regeneration and quad origins are much higher, at +848. Some source rewards depend on traversal or mode conditions that these sections alone do not resolve. Voyager 2 has thirteen deathmatch starts at three origin heights, two body armors at +480 and +686, and 809 patch surfaces omitted from brush reconstruction.

Application: investigate how a route grants access to a reward and how the player returns to combat; never copy an isolated high pickup without its access rules. Use Voyager 2’s multi-height evidence as a prompt for in-engine review, not as a complete floor plan: it is the most patch-heavy source in this collection.

Altar and Blast Radius — spatial contrast before decoration

Section observations: Altar’s lower narrow run expands into a more branched upper footprint around a substantial central obstruction. Blast Radius presents a broader lobe connected to narrower peripheral space, with columns and height-dependent obstructions.

Application: build a memorable contrast between compressed approaches and a larger encounter volume. Let that contrast establish weapon opportunities and orientation. A succession of equally wide lanes with freestanding cover would miss this lesson.

A practical design process for Fragony

Start with this game’s dimensions and combat

Current base walking speed is 7.5 m/s, sprint target 11 m/s, body diameter 0.8 m, standing height 1.9 m and ordinary step allowance 0.3 m. Jump launch speed 8.5 m/s with gravity 23 m/s² gives an ideal apex of 1.57 m and equal-height flight of 0.739 s. At constant base speeds, that is approximately 5.54 m walking or 8.13 m sprinting horizontally. These are ballistic reference values; acceleration, body radius, headroom, air control, attachments and collision reduce or change practical clearance. Reservoir uses a special 0.57 m step allowance. Keep ordinary routes playable without a rocket jump.

Design close corners for shotgun and SMG pressure, medium spaces for rifle and hand-cannon exchange, and selected longer angles for the piercing rail. Rockets and grenades punish static cover and confined exits. A corridor that protects against one weapon can become a splash trap. Randomized two-weapon loadouts require viable alternate approaches rather than a mandatory weapon-specific crossing.

Block out, compare, then detail

  1. Write the encounter brief: six-player FFA, 90 seconds, one principal contest, a recovery circuit and a counter-route. Name a spatial identity for each major region.
  2. Build two meaningfully different blockouts: for example a compact stacked loop and a longer offset two-lobe loop. Place the three allowed health types early. Compare route decisions rather than decorative treatments.
  3. Draw a directed route graph: annotate walking time, exposure, height, drop commitment, lift delay and any special movement requirement. Two doors into the same watched corridor count as one tactical approach until proven otherwise.
  4. Walk it in first person: check every threshold, stair, low ceiling, landing, diagonal corner and escape. Inspect at eye height as well as in plan. Verify whether the player sees a destination before committing.
  5. Run equal-population trials: compare the same bot seeds, player starting regions and early/late loadouts. Record time to first visible opponent, travel to useful cover, pickup collection/denial, regional occupancy, repeated spawn deaths and route completion. Human sessions must assess orientation and enjoyable decisions.
  6. Change the weakest decision: if a branch is unused, investigate access cost, reward value, visibility, target selection and competing routes. Add geometry only after identifying the cause.

Review gates before committing to art

  • Exactly one 50 HP pickup; every fragment and recovery pack follows the required overheal rule.
  • At least two tactically distinct ways to contest the major, plus a usable departure; verify with actual sightlines and travel, not door count.
  • No single perch simultaneously controls the major, safe sustain, all approaches and its own escape.
  • Injured players can reach a 25 HP recovery opportunity and rejoin circulation; full-health players have useful rotation choices through fragments.
  • Every ordinary route and spawn works for player and bots, including collision, stance, stairs, lift waits, drops and water where applicable.
  • All intended major regions are used during sustained play; lopsided use has an explained tactical purpose. Seek useful differences, not equal occupancy.
  • Deaths near a spawn, long empty walks and repeated backtracking are reviewed against recordings. Treat any numerical timing target as a playtest hypothesis until measured.

No new gameplay, maps or deployments were made during this study. The next implementation should reference these gates and the source evidence rather than treating the map names as a style guide.

How to interpret the evidence

This is a source and geometry study, not a playthrough of every map. The analyzer reads all 19 Radiant sources, counts entities and brushes, retains source hashes, and reconstructs convex brush intersections at selected heights. It also decodes the supplied EF1 IBSP v46 and EF2! v20 BSP collision records. Full raw evidence, entity keys, coordinates and brush planes are in evidence.json; analysis and document generation are reproducible from the adjacent Python files.

Missing elements include curved patch geometry in source maps, compiled visual faces, texture/shader behavior, dynamic entity transforms, scripted movement and game-mode activation. Brush geometry is not a verified navigation graph. A straight-line distance is a lower bound, not a travel time. Source brush counts and compiled collision-brush counts are different representations and must not be used to rank map complexity. Native height origins are often above the actual floor. The 1/32 scale is the current Reservoir port’s conversion, not a universal Elite Force scale prescription.

The standalone files are local research artifacts and are not included in the game’s dist directory. Original package readmes are attribution and context, not instructions to install packages, run commands or contact their authors.

Sources

  • Supplied 19 .map sources in eliteforce_holomatch_maps, plus the two PK3 archives and their readmes. Individual source paths and SHA-256 hashes are retained in evidence.json.
  • Josh Foreman — Level Design for PvP FPS: designer’s account of sightline risk, landmarks and iteration.
  • Spearmint EF2 BSP loader and ioquake3 BSP structures: primary format references.
  • Local Fragony files: dist/pickups.js, dist/feel.js, dist/collision.js, dist/game.js, dist/maps/reservoir.js; earlier flow observations in workspace findings.md. Prior test results are historical evidence, not rerun results from this study.
